decisions.quote: An initial study analyzing two small‐scale field experiments argued that describing someone as a voter (noun) instead of one who votes (verb) increases turnout rates 11 to 14 points because the noun activates a person's social identity as a voter. A subsequent study analyzing a large‐scale field experiment challenged this claim and found no effect.
decisions.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The supplied primary source is an abstract only and describes a large-scale field experiment retesting the claim from an unnamed 'initial study analyzing two small-scale field experiments' that noun ('voter') versus verb ('votes') wording increases voter turnout by 11 to 14 percentage points by invoking the self, following an unnamed 'subsequent study analyzing a large-scale field experiment' that found no effect. Because the abstract includes no author names, publication years, titles, or reference list, primary-source evidence cannot establish the bibliographic identity of target_index 0 from the text itself or verify whether shipped row 1760 (Bryan, Walton, Rogers, & Dweck, 2011, 'Motivating voter turnout by invoking the self', DOI 10.1073/pnas.1103343108) already represents this initial study (contrary to Luna's unsupported assumption that row 1760 is the later study) or whether the subsequent large-scale study is also a replication-chain target in the full text.
